cards.title: Engineering Brief — C-Clamp Screw and Collar Friction Analysis
cards.body: A C-clamp is a portable mechanical clamping tool used extensively in manufacturing, fabrication, welding, and woodworking. You are required to analyse the power screw mechanism of a multi-start thread C-clamp, determine the thread friction torque and collar friction torque, evaluate the total tightening torque required to achieve a specified clamping load, and quantify the significant contribution of collar friction to overall operator effort.

cards.title: C-Clamp Operating Principle — Dual Friction Resistance
cards.body:
A C-clamp power screw converts rotary effort at the sliding handle into controlled axial clamping force on the workpiece.

Mechanical Load Path:
  Handle Rotation → Screw Rotation → Helical Thread Engagement → Axial Screw Translation → Pressure Pad Thrust → Clamping Force (W)

Dual Friction Interfaces:
  1. Thread Friction (Tₛ): Friction generated between the external threads of the power screw and the internal threads in the C-clamp frame.
  2. Collar Friction (T꜀): Friction generated at the thrust collar interface between the screw end and the swiveling pressure pad.

Total Tightening Torque Relation:
  T_total = Tₛ + T꜀

where:
  Tₛ = (W · dₘ / 2) · [ (μ + tan α) / (1 − μ · tan α) ]
  T꜀ = μ_c · W · (d_c / 2)

Key Distinction (Pitch vs Lead for Multi-Start Screws):
  Pitch (p): Distance between consecutive thread crests.
  Lead (L): Distance the screw advances axially per revolution (L = n × p, where n is number of starts).
  For a two-start screw (n = 2): L = 2p.

cards.title: Engineering Objectives
items: Identify the key C-clamp components and friction interfaces on Engineering Asset EA-19.
Trace the rotary-to-linear load transmission path from handle to workpiece.
Distinguish clearly between thread pitch (p) and screw lead (L) for a two-start power screw.
Calculate mean screw diameter (dₘ) and helix angle (α).
Compute thread friction torque (Tₛ) using square-thread power-screw equations.
Compute collar friction torque (T꜀) at the pressure pad thrust interface.
Determine total tightening torque (T_total) and required operator hand force (F).
Analyse the percentage increase in total torque caused by collar friction.
Formulate technically justified engineering recommendations regarding lubrication, collar design, and handle length.

component-identification.title: Identify C-Clamp Components and Mechanical Functions
component-identification.description: Engineering asset illustrating a conventional C-clamp power-screw mechanism with identified structural parts, force vectors, and friction interfaces.

labels.feedback: The fixed upper anvil forms the stationary reaction face of the rigid C-clamp frame.
The workpiece is clamped between the upper anvil and the pressure pad.
The rigid C-frame resists bending moments and tensile loads.
The pressure pad swivels on the screw end collar, distributing clamping force.
The power screw transmits input torque and advances axially.
Helical threads convert rotational motion to axial translation.
The internal threaded nut portion of the frame where thread friction torque (Tₛ) is generated.
The thrust interface between screw tip and pressure pad where collar friction (T꜀) acts.
The enlarged boss at the lower end containing the sliding handle.
The sliding tommy-bar handle provides the lever arm (R) for applying tightening torque.

motion-sequence.title: Understand the Power-Screw Load and Motion Path
motion-sequence.prompt: Analyse how rotational effort applied by the operator at the handle is converted into clamping force on the workpiece in Engineering Asset EA-19.

mcq.question: Which sequence correctly describes the complete mechanical load path and motion transformation in a C-clamp power screw?

options.label: Tangential force applied at handle → Torque applied to screw head → Power screw rotates in frame threads → Helical engagement converts rotation into axial movement → Pressure pad advances against workpiece → Clamping load (W) generated
Pressure pad moves independently → Handle rotates as a reaction → Screw thread expands → Frame contracts onto workpiece
Screw rotates without axial movement → Frame stretches outward → Fixed anvil pushes workpiece against pressure pad → Handle slides sideways
Workpiece deformation rotates the screw → Screw advances handle downward → Collar friction creates clamping load directly

design-data.title: Establish Design Data and Engineering Assumptions
design-data.prompt: Confirm all given engineering parameters for the EA-19 C-clamp power screw mechanism prior to conducting torque calculations.

mcq.question: Which set of design parameters correctly represents the complete given data for the EA-19 C-clamp mechanism?

options.label: Clamping load W = 5,000 N | Nominal diameter d = 22 mm | Pitch p = 5 mm | Number of starts n = 2 | Lead L = 10 mm | Thread friction μ = 0.15 | Collar friction μ_c = 0.10 | Mean collar diameter d_c = 28 mm | Handle radius R = 120 mm
Clamping load W = 5,000 N | d = 22 mm | p = 5 mm | Single-start (n = 1, L = 5 mm) | μ = 0.15 | μ_c = 0.10 | d_c = 28 mm | R = 120 mm
Clamping load W = 10,000 N | d = 30 mm | p = 6 mm | Double-start (L = 12 mm) | μ = 0.20 | μ_c = 0.15 | d_c = 40 mm | R = 200 mm
Clamping load W = 5,000 N | d = 22 mm | p = 10 mm | Triple-start (L = 30 mm) | μ = 0.08 | μ_c = 0.05 | d_c = 20 mm | R = 100 mm

screw-geometry.title: Determine Screw Geometry and Helix Angle
screw-geometry.prompt:
For a square-thread power screw:
  Mean Screw Diameter:  dₘ = d − (p / 2)
  Lead (two-start):     L = n × p = 2 × 5 = 10 mm
  Helix Angle:          tan α = L / (π · dₘ)

Given Data:
  d = 22 mm,   p = 5 mm,   n = 2 (Two-Start Thread)

Calculate the mean screw diameter (dₘ), lead (L), and helix angle (α).

mcq.question: What are the correct mean screw diameter (dₘ), lead (L), and helix angle (α) for the two-start C-clamp screw?

thread-torque.title: Calculate Thread Friction Torque
thread-torque.prompt:
For a square-thread power screw, the torque required to raise the clamping load (overcome thread friction) is:

  Tₛ = (W · dₘ / 2) · [ (μ + tan α) / (1 − μ · tan α) ]

where:
  W     = 5,000 N       (Clamping Load)
  dₘ    = 19.5 mm       (Mean Screw Diameter)
  μ     = 0.15          (Thread Friction Coefficient)
  tan α = 0.16324       (α ≈ 9.27°)

Calculate the thread friction angle φ = tan⁻¹(μ) and thread friction torque Tₛ (in N·mm).

mcq.question: What is the correct thread friction torque Tₛ for the C-clamp power screw?

options.label: Tₛ = W · dₘ · μ = 5,000 × 19.5 × 0.15 = 14,625 N·mm  (friction force only — helix angle α omitted)
Tₛ = (W · dₘ / 2) · tan α = 48,750 × 0.16324 = 7,958 N·mm  (ideal load component without friction)
Tₛ = (W · L) / (2π) = (5,000 × 10) / (2π) = 50,000 / 6.2832 ≈ 7,958 N·mm  (zero-friction efficiency relation)

collar-torque.title: Calculate Collar Friction Torque
collar-torque.prompt:
Collar friction torque accounts for friction at the thrust interface between the rotating screw tip and non-rotating pressure pad:

  T_c = μ_c · W · (d_c / 2)

where:
  μ_c = 0.10     (Collar Friction Coefficient)
  W   = 5,000 N  (Clamping Load)
  d_c = 28 mm    (Mean Collar Diameter)

Calculate the collar friction torque T_c in N·mm and N·m.

mcq.question: What is the correct collar friction torque T_c for the C-clamp mechanism?

options.label: T_c = (μ_c · W) / d_c = (0.10 × 5,000) / 28 = 17.86 N·mm  (inverted collar radius)
T_c = μ_c · (d_c / 2) = 0.10 × 14 = 1.4 N·mm  (forgot clamping load W)

total-torque-force.title: Determine Total Tightening Torque and Operator Hand Force
total-torque-force.prompt:
Total Tightening Torque:
  T_total = Tₛ + T_c

Required Operator Hand Force at Handle:
  F = T_total / R

Given:
  Tₛ ≈ 15,654 N·mm,   T_c = 7,000 N·mm,   Handle Radius R = 120 mm (0.12 m)

Calculate total tightening torque T_total (in N·mm and N·m) and required operator hand force F (in N).

mcq.question: What are the correct total tightening torque T_total and required operator hand force F?

options.label: T_total = Tₛ = 15,654 N·mm  (collar friction omitted)  |  F = 15,654 / 120 ≈ 130.5 N
T_total = T_c = 7,000 N·mm  (thread friction omitted)  |  F = 7,000 / 120 ≈ 58.3 N

collar-friction-effect.title: Analyse the Relative Effect and Significance of Collar Friction
collar-friction-effect.prompt:
Investigate how collar friction increases the required operator tightening torque compared to thread friction alone.

  Case A (Without Collar Friction):  T_without = Tₛ = 15,654 N·mm
  Case B (With Collar Friction):     T_with = T_total = 22,654 N·mm
  Increase due to Collar Friction:   ΔT = T_c = 7,000 N·mm

Calculate the percentage increase in tightening torque caused by collar friction over thread torque alone, and its proportion of total torque.

mcq.question: Which evaluation accurately quantifies the impact of collar friction on C-clamp tightening torque?

options.label: Percentage increase over thread torque = (T_c / Tₛ) × 100% = (7,000 / 15,654) × 100% ≈ 44.72%  |  Proportion of total torque = (T_c / T_total) × 100% = (7,000 / 22,654) × 100% ≈ 30.90%  |  Conclusion: Collar friction increases tightening torque by ~44.7% and accounts for nearly 1/3 of total operator effort; ignoring it causes severe torque underestimation.
Percentage increase = (T_c / T_total) × 100% = 7,000 / 22,654 × 100% = 3.09%  (decimal error)  |  Conclusion: Collar friction is negligible.
Percentage increase = (T_s / T_c) × 100% = 15,654 / 7,000 × 100% = 223.6%  |  Conclusion: Thread friction is smaller than collar friction.
Percentage increase = 0%  |  Conclusion: Collar friction and thread friction cancel each other out completely.

options.title: C-CLAMP DESIGN IS ACCEPTABLE — SELF-LOCKING CONFIRMED, OPERATOR FORCE WITHIN PRACTICAL LIMITS
options.description: The two-start C-clamp power screw achieves a 5 kN clamping force with an operator hand force of ~188.8 N at R = 120 mm handle, which is well within practical manual operating capability (~200 N limit). The thread friction angle (φ ≈ 8.53°) and helix angle (α ≈ 9.27°) maintain effective clamping function without spontaneous back-driving under vibration due to collar friction resistance. Regular application of grease at the thrust pad collar maintains μ_c ≤ 0.10, preventing premature wear and galling.

options.title: DESIGN MODIFICATION RECOMMENDED — REDUCE COLLAR FRICTION VIA THRUST WASHER OR EXTEND HANDLE
options.description: Because collar friction accounts for nearly 31% of the total tightening torque (7,000 N·mm out of 22,654 N·mm), operating effort can be significantly reduced by introducing a bronze thrust washer or needle roller thrust bearing at the pressure pad interface (reducing μ_c from 0.10 to 0.04). Alternatively, extending the sliding handle radius from 120 mm to 150 mm reduces operator hand force from 188.8 N to 151.0 N, improving ergonomics and reducing operator fatigue during repetitive industrial clamping.
